content.title: Europe needs more of its own energy – wind and sun are not enough
content.lead: Four years after the invasion of Ukraine, the Iran war once again exposes Europe's strategic vulnerability: The continent produces too little energy. This creates dangerous dependencies and does nothing for the climate.

content.text: The repercussions of the Iran war are reaching all continents like a tsunami. They are being transmitted via the shipping routes of the large oil and liquefied gas tankers, which have been disrupted for more than a month by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Even if the war and the blockade are ended through negotiations in the coming weeks, one thing is already clear: the Israeli and US attack on Iran will lead to a surge in global inflation, dampening economic growth. The wholesale price of natural gas in Europe is around 50 percent higher for the remainder of the year than before the war. Gasoline has become 12 percent more expensive on average, and diesel 26 percent more expensive. In the best-case scenario of a swift reopening of trade, the International Monetary Fund projects a 0.3 percent slowdown in global growth.

content.text: The obvious answer to the recent oil crisis might seem to be to accelerate the electrification of economies through electricity from renewable energy sources. Europe wants to leave the fossil fuel age behind with all its crises and dependencies. This strategy remains correct, but for now it is a dream. Despite significant progress in the installation and use of wind and solar power, the use of fossil fuels in Europe, while declining, is indispensable. And this will remain the case for many years to come.

Wind and solar energy reached a record high share of electricity production across Europe in 2025, at 30% – one percentage point more than fossil fuels. However, Europe as a whole still needs fossil fuels. In 2024, only 20% of total energy consumption came from renewable sources, compared to 38% from oil, 21% from natural gas and 10% from coal. Europe has to import 57% of its energy needs.

content.text: A rapid shift away from fossil fuels is unrealistic. In Great Britain, for example, three-quarters of private households still heat their homes with gas burners, and there is no realistic plan to change this in the short term. And despite the planned ban on coal-fired power plants by 2038, Germany burns more coal for electricity generation than any other European country. Economics Minister Katherina Reiche therefore wants to build new gas-fired power plants with a capacity of at least 11 gigawatts. This is roughly the same output as the eight nuclear power plants that were taken offline in Germany in the last 10 years. The new gas-fired power plants are necessary because electricity production from wind and solar power fluctuates considerably. The situation is similar in Switzerland, which will find it difficult to avoid building several gas-fired power plants due to its growing electricity demand.

content.title: Successes and shortcomings of climate policy

content.text: Under the U.N. climate agreements, European states have committed to a further drastic reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, aiming to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 at the latest. However, Europe is far from reaching this goal, and the rest of the world is even further behind. Global warming compared to pre-industrial levels has already reached 1.5 degrees, a threshold that, according to the 2015 Paris Agreement, was not supposed to be exceeded by the end of the century. Realistically, the best hope now is that warming remains within the range of 2 to 3 degrees in the long term.

Historically, the West has released by far the largest quantities of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere due to its significant head start in industrialization and its high level of prosperity. Climate activists rightly derive from this a moral obligation to take the lead in climate protection. The West has also achieved a great deal since the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. Economic growth has been decoupled from emissions. In 2024, emissions in Europe were around 40% lower than in 1990.

content.text: But with Donald Trump's return to the White House, the U.S. withdrew from all climate policy commitments. National regulation of greenhouse gases was halted. Instead, the production of natural gas and oil is being accelerated. Trump is obsessively fighting the further installation of wind and solar power plants.

And even in Europe, it's doubtful how strong the will and willingness to make sacrifices for the goal of climate neutrality actually are. While there's no lack of abstract support for climate protection, which is also reflected in legislation, citizens' consumption patterns offer little evidence of this. The much-discussed «flight shame» of the climate strike era is a figment of the imagination. If a country cuts subsidies for electric cars, solar panels, or heat pumps, demand collapses.

There have also been recent setbacks at the political level. The emissions trading system for large consumers is under attack from various governments. The new German government has weakened overly costly and unpopular regulations for building heating systems. While it remains committed to the goal of climate neutrality by 2045, the country is not on track, according to the German Council of Experts on Climate Change. In several countries, including Italy and Germany, governments could not withstand the pressure of rising fuel prices for even a few weeks and quickly moved to cut taxes. The fact that this undermines a price signal that could incentivize the switch to electric vehicles is apparently of secondary importance.

It is high time that European energy policy adopts a more realistic self-assessment. Further reducing greenhouse gases is a valid goal. Climate change poses risks that affect everyone and should not be accepted without action. However, it is not crucial whether Europe achieves climate neutrality a few years earlier or later – especially since the rest of the world, responsible for roughly 90% of emissions, is not following Europe's lead anyway. What is crucial is that the energy transition, with all its consequences, is accepted and supported by society and the economy.

Electricity demand will rise sharply in the coming years, driven by the electrification of transportation, building heating, industry and booming data centers. Growth in Europe is estimated at more than 2% per year. Renewable energies are insufficient to meet this demand, both now and in the foreseeable future, partly due to a lack of storage capacity. If gas is scarce or too expensive, decommissioned coal-fired power plants will be reactivated as a last resort (as happened after Russia's invasion of Ukraine) – the worst-case scenario for the climate. In the U.S., on the other hand, growing electricity demand is primarily met by more climate-friendly gas-fired power plants, thanks to abundant natural gas and gas prices that, even before the Iran war, were only about one-third as high as in Europe. These low gas prices impact electricity prices, which are roughly half as high for large consumers in the U.S. as in Europe.

It does nothing for the climate to relocate industrial production to other continents where energy prices are lower due to less stringent climate protection requirements. Despite government subsidies, high energy prices for industry and the extremely expensive programs to replace natural gas with (non-existent) hydrogen are driving too many companies out of Europe.
On the path to climate neutrality, Europe should therefore pay more attention to security of supply and costs, in addition to climate protection. The following adjustments are important:

Natural gas production in Europe (excluding Norway) has fallen by around 70% in the last 20 years. This is not solely due to the depletion of the large North Sea fields. It also results from a widespread reluctance to invest in new exploration, which is hampered by high taxes and a lack of government permits due to climate protection concerns; this is currently the subject of intense political debate in Great Britain. Eight European countries have banned oil and gas extraction through fracking. Yet, fracking has made the U.S. the world's largest producer and a net exporter over the last 15 years. The potential of geothermal energy is also being explored more extensively in the U.S. than in Europe. However, Europe's reluctance does not mean it consumes less gas, gasoline and diesel; these fuels are simply imported, increasingly from the U.S. The Iran war and the tensions with the extortionate Trump administration show how vulnerable this dependence makes Europe. More domestic natural gas production would not decouple the continent from global market prices, but it would improve security of supply and reduce its susceptibility to political blackmail. That would be important in the new age of geopolitical brutality.

The European Commission is now calling for a revival of nuclear energy. This is a good thing. However, by the time new nuclear power plants are operational in Europe – whether conventional or the new modular reactors – the continent will be well into the 2030s. This makes it all the more important that Europe quickly embraces this technology.

Renewable energies are proving their worth. However, for their further expansion, the structural prerequisites must be created in a timely manner and at reasonable costs. The expansion of wind and solar power must go hand in hand with the expansion of the distribution networks and must not overload them. Therefore, the proposals of German Economics Minister Katherina Reiche are correct, for example, to discontinue subsidies for rooftop solar panels and to limit the purchase guarantees for new wind turbines where adequate grid connection is lacking. This is intended to avoid disproportionate costs.

Electric vehicles are the future. However, their success should not depend on subsidies. Instead, solutions are needed for expanding the charging infrastructure, including for apartment renters without garage spaces. With the latest innovations in battery technology that will come onto the market in the next few years, electric vehicles will very soon be attractive and competitive even without subsidies – provided the charging infrastructure is available for the mass market. For this reason, current subsidy programs do not make sense.

Europe must not lose sight of climate protection; it is crucial. Precisely for this reason, policymakers should adopt a more sensible course and create the conditions for success under economic conditions. Otherwise, the already visible backlash threatens to intensify dangerously. Consumers' willingness to make sacrifices is strictly limited. The same applies to the endurance of businesses. Political slogans and persistent lobbying alone will not achieve climate goals.

newestTopComments.text: It seems to be a law of nature that energy is significantly more expensive in Europe than in the USA. If the tax difference per liter were invested in expanding renewable energies, and especially in distribution networks, storage, and charging infrastructure, the situation would look very different. Unfortunately, these funds were spent elsewhere, quite sensibly, of course. The fact that relocating energy-intensive production abroad doesn't slow the temperature rise hasn't yet sunk in for every Green Party member. There's an enormous amount of hypocrisy involved in this whole issue

I read with some amusement the comments here that deny the negative impact of CO2 and, presumably, global warming as well. Both exist. And those who deny the facts will be cursed by their children and grandchildren. I can best understand the criticism of climate policy insofar as its implementation in Germany and the EU has been, and continues to be, clumsy and damaging to the economic balance. In my opinion, the blame lies both with the Greens, whose radicalism disregards the economy, and with those within the EU who – more for geostrategic reasons – are pretending to be green. That has failed. One should realize that Germany has been, and is, dependent on raw materials. And will continue to be to a considerable extent. How to proceed intelligently in such matters can be seen – once again – in China: restructuring the energy system at a reasonable pace – while maintaining coal/gas and nuclear power. Which brings us to the major problems in the EU and Germany: the, in my opinion, very low quality of the political personnel in charge. And significant portions of the population who are unable to make an objectively justified decision in elections.
